keyVerseText: And Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pashur, the son of Malchijah, and Maasiai the son of Adiel, the son of Jahzerah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Meshillemith, the son of Immer;
rootMeaning: The root of יַחְזֵרָה (Yachzêrâh) is linked to חֲזִיר (chăzîyr), which primarily means 'boar' or 'swine.' While this root might suggest something untamed or wild, the etymology hints at a meaning related to protection or perhaps a guarded enclosure, as swine could be penned or protected animals. This dual sense enriches the understanding of the name beyond a mere proper noun, suggesting one who is under divine guidance or care, consistent with the gloss 'whom God leads back.'
usageInScripture: The word יַחְזֵרָה appears only once in Scripture, specifically in 1 Chronicles 9:12, where it is used as a proper name referring to an Israelite priest of the house of Immer. The consistent translation 'of Jahzerah' underscores its function as a family or clan name rather than a descriptive term. This singular occurrence emphasizes its role in identifying a priestly lineage, reflecting the importance of genealogical records in maintaining the covenant community's religious identity.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding יַחְזֵרָה as a name meaning 'whom God leads back' invites reflection on God's providential guidance and restoration of His people. The priestly connection highlights God's provision of mediators who lead His people in worship and covenant faithfulness. From a Christ-centered perspective, this name prefigures the ultimate High Priest who perfectly leads sinners back to God. The protective nuance in the root suggests God's safeguarding of His covenant community, reinforcing themes of divine care and leadership throughout redemptive history.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Chronicles 9:12, יַחְזֵרָה identifies a priestly ancestor in the lineage of those serving in Jerusalem. The mention of 'Maasiai the son of Adiel, the son of Jahzerah' situates this individual within a faithful priestly heritage. The name's meaning, 'whom God leads back,' enriches the verse by reminding readers that these priests were part of God's ongoing work to restore and maintain His people, especially in the post-exilic period when the community was reestablishing worship and identity.
